You express change at B2 level by choosing the right verb for “to become”: ponerse (momentary change), volverse (change of character), hacerse (deliberate change), convertirse en (transformation), llegar a ser (after a long road) and quedarse (the result of an event).
to grow old, to grow up
to end up being, to become (eventually)
Andrei went red when he read the email.
Since the operation, Ecaterina has become very demanding.
I want to become a professional photographer.
The café has turned into a small library.
To use “ponerse + adjective” for quick, passing changes (ponerse nervioso, rojo, triste).
To use “volverse + adjective” for changes of character, often unexpected (volverse exigente, desconfiado).
To use “hacerse + noun/adjective” for deliberate or gradual changes (hacerse fotógrafo, rico, mayor).
To use “convertirse en”, “llegar a ser” and “quedarse + adjective” for transformations, achievements after effort and results of an event.
To avoid translating “to become” mechanically and choose the verb according to the type of change.
Thursday, 15 July, evening, Bucharest. It’s very hot. The club has gathered on Ecaterina’s balcony. Ecaterina suggests a game: each person says what they have turned into this year.
I suggest a game. Each of you says what you’ve turned into this year. I’ll start: I’ve become demanding. Since the operation I can see the dust on the furniture and it gets on my nerves.
Well, I’ve become a student. At my age. I’ve signed up for the DELE B2 exam in November.
Costel! And you hadn’t told us?
I was embarrassed. Every time I talk about it, I go red. Look, I’m already going red.
I’ve got some news, but I don’t know yet if it’s good. A photography agency in Madrid has offered me a six-month internship. From September.
Because of the photo from the fair?
Yes. When I read the email, I was left speechless. But my father has always wanted me to become an engineer, like him.
Lad, your father cried on the phone when he saw the photo in the paper. He told me himself.
Andrei, nobody becomes what they want without making a few mistakes. Go to Madrid. And if you go mad, come back.
OK. But first I’ll tell my father. If I keep quiet another week, I really will go mad.
“me pongo nerviosa” = I get worked up
“me he inscrito” = I have signed up
“me estoy poniendo rojo” = I’m going red
“me quedé sin palabras” = I was left speechless
“que me hiciera ingeniero” = that I become an engineer
The diphthong “ue” is stressed in the present and participle forms: VUEL-to, VUEL-ve. In the infinitive it disappears: vol-VER-se. Don’t say “vuolto”.
“puso” has a single, voiceless “s”: PU-so. Don’t confuse it with “pozo” (well), where the “z” is [θ] in Spain.
It is linked into a single group: [lle-GA-ra-SER]. The “a” attaches to “llegar”.
1. English has “become”, Spanish has six verbs
In English we mostly say “become” or “get”. In Spanish you choose the verb according to the TYPE of change:
Me pongo nerviosa. Se puso rojo.
Se hizo fotógrafo. Nos hacemos mayores.
El café se convirtió en una biblioteca.
the result of an event (often a loss)
Se quedó viudo. Me quedé sin palabras.
Costel goes red every time he talks about the exam.
When he saw the photo, his father was really pleased.
Over the years, he became distrustful.
If I keep quiet, I’ll go mad.
Trick: if the change could pass by this evening, it’s “ponerse”. If it stays part of who someone is, it’s “volverse”.
3. Hacerse, convertirse en, llegar a ser
Ecaterina turned into a writer one night in July.
After twenty years, he became site manager.
“Hacerse” is also used for ideologies and religions (hacerse vegetariano, budista) and in fixed expressions: «Se hace tarde» (it’s getting late), «hacerse mayor» (to grow old / to grow up).
Andrés was widowed when Pilar was little.
When I read the email, I was left speechless.
The premises were left empty for years.
“Quedarse” describes the state you are left in AFTER something: quedarse ciego, sordo, sin trabajo, embarazada, tranquilo, solo.
“When he saw him, he got sad.” (momentary)
Cuando lo vio, se puso triste.
Cuando lo vio, se hizo triste.
Cuando lo vio, llegó a ser triste.

¿A qué examen se ha inscrito Costel?

An email from Lola to the club, at the end of July. Notice the verbs of change.
Dear friends in Bucharest, I’m writing to tell you that the café has turned into something else. Since we put the books from the funeral on the shelves, people no longer come just for coffee.
They come to read, they take a book and bring it back a week later, sometimes with a note inside. Without realising it, I’ve become a librarian. My mother says I’ve turned into a romantic.
Yesterday a little boy burst into tears because he didn’t want to give back a book about pirates. I gave it to him. I think Señor Andrés would have done the same.
The lamp at the back is still lit every night. Some neighbours already call it “Andrés’s lamp”. A big hug. Lola.

That July, Bucharest turned into an oven. The thermometers outside the chemists’ showed thirty-nine degrees at six in the evening, the asphalt went soft underfoot and the lime trees on the boulevard had already lost their scent. Ecaterina had her second eye operated on on the 8th. This time she didn’t cry when the bandage came off. She merely looked around with a critical expression and said the hospital room needed a coat of paint.

With both eyes new, she became unbearably demanding. She saw the dust on the books, the smudges on the windows, the crooked pictures and the spelling mistakes on shop signs. She phoned the bakery on her street to point out that the window said “croasant” instead of “croissant”. Ana told her she had been nicer before the operation. Ecaterina replied that before the operation she had been blinder, which is not the same thing.

One afternoon, while tidying the bookcase in the living room, she found a shoebox full of photos of Madrid from the eighties. For years she hadn’t looked at them, because she saw them blurred and because she didn’t dare. Now she saw them with an almost cruel clarity. In one of them was she herself, in her thirties, with long hair, in front of the green sign, laughing at something outside the frame. On the back, in Andrés’s handwriting, it said: “E., who never keeps still. 1983.” She sat on the floor with the photo in her hand until it got dark.

On Thursday evenings, when the heat eased a little, the club met on her balcony, among pots of geraniums and a folding table Mihai had brought up from the basement. There was lemonade, cold watermelon and, sometimes, Mrs Florica’s soup, since she had decided the club was her business. It was on one of those Thursdays, 15 July, that Ecaterina suggested the game: each of them had to tell what they had turned into that year.

Costel surprised everyone the most. He had signed up for the DELE B2 exam in November, at the Instituto Cervantes, without telling anyone. He had done it in a car park in Slovakia, on his phone, at two in the morning, in a fit of courage that had lasted exactly long enough to pay the fee. The next day he had woken up terrified, but there was no backing out.

He had also talked to his boss. He had asked for shorter routes, within Romania or, at most, as far as Hungary, so he could sleep at home at least three nights a week. His boss had turned serious, looked at the blue book Costel always kept in the cab and said yes. Costel explained that he wanted to study at a real table, not on the steering wheel. Mrs Florica, who was serving the soup, said it was about time.

His study method had become famous at the company. He had vocabulary cards stuck all over the dashboard, recorded audio messages in which he asked himself questions and, during compulsory breaks, did reading-comprehension exercises sitting on the lorry’s steps. Zoltán tested him over the CB radio from Hungary, although he knew only thirty words of Spanish and half of them were about food. Even so, Costel said he was the most demanding teacher he had ever had.

Then it was Andrei’s turn; he had been quiet all afternoon, eating watermelon without appetite. He said that a week after the fair he had received an email from a photography agency in Madrid. They had seen the photo in the paper and were offering him a six-month internship, with a small salary, starting in September. When he read it, he was left speechless. He read it five times, in case he had misunderstood. Then he closed the computer and told nobody for six weeks.

The problem was his father. Señor Dan had built bridges for thirty-five years and had always taken it for granted that his son would become an engineer, like him, like his grandfather. Andrei had started an engineering degree because of that, and had dropped out in the second year, also because of that. Since then there had been a polite silence between father and son, the kind that makes no noise but takes up a lot of room at the table.

Costel reminded everyone that Señor Dan had cried on the phone when he saw the photo in the paper. Andrei hadn’t known. He went red, then pale, and then said he had to go. Ecaterina walked him to the door. There she told him that nobody becomes what they want without making a few mistakes, and that if he went mad in Madrid, he could always come back. Andrei kissed her on the cheek, something he had never done, and ran down the stairs.

That same night he went to see his father. He found him in the garage, fixing an old bicycle nobody used. Andrei showed him the email on his phone without a word. Señor Dan read it twice, his glasses on the tip of his nose, just like Ecaterina. Then he put the spanner down on the table, wiped his hands on a rag and stood looking at the bicycle for a long time.

“I became an engineer because my father wanted me to,” he said at last. “And I don’t regret it, because I like bridges. But it took me twenty years to become a good engineer, and in those twenty years nobody asked me what I wanted.” He paused. “You become whatever you want. But become good at it.” Then he asked him to explain what exactly a photography agency was, how much a flat in Madrid cost and whether photos were measured in pixels or centimetres.

That night, very late, father and son went out for a walk. Without agreeing on it, they ended up on a bridge over the Dâmbovița that Señor Dan had designed at thirty. His father told him that the night before it opened to traffic he hadn’t slept at all; that at six in the morning he had gone to watch the first lorry cross, and had started shaking like a child. “Fear doesn’t go away,” he told him. “You get used to crossing with it.” Andrei took a photo of the bridge with his phone. It was the first photo his father ever asked him to send.

Andrei accepted the internship the next day. Marta wrote to him at once to offer him the room off the hallway in the flat on the calle del Prado, where she now lived alone. She said the flat had become too big and too quiet, and that a photographer who got up early would do her good. Andrei asked if he could hang his photos in the hallway. Marta said yes, as long as he didn’t touch the green sign.

When Andrei told the club, Mihai said they would be left without an official photographer and that from now on the Thursday photos would all come out blurred. Ana, on the other hand, turned practical: she wrote him a list of useful addresses in Lavapiés and called her mother. Half an hour later, Carmen had already called Andrei to ask whether he ate his tortilla with or without onion. Andrei, who had learnt his lesson at the fair, said with onion. Carmen said in that case she was adopting him.

The one who didn’t want to play the balcony game was Ecaterina herself. When they asked her what she had turned into, apart from a demanding person, she changed the subject and went to the kitchen for more lemonade. But that same week, Marta called her from Madrid with a proposal. First she asked her for the final text for the plaque, which had to be sent to the city council before 31 July. Then, very carefully, she asked whether she had ever thought of writing her own version of the story.

Ecaterina got defensive. She said she was a translator, not a writer; that she had spent her life putting other people’s words into Romanian, and that at her age you don’t turn into something else. Marta reminded her that the novel told only what her grandfather remembered. The other half was missing: that of the woman who left one autumn day, who wrote a letter and didn’t send it, who waited forty years in Bucharest.

Ecaterina said no. She said it twice, very firmly. Then she hung up, sat down at the computer, opened the blank document she hadn’t touched for a month and wrote one sentence: “I arrived in Madrid in 1977 with a suitcase, a dictionary and the absolute certainty that I would soon leave.” She looked at it for a long time. She didn’t like it. She deleted it. She wrote it again exactly the same. It was three in the morning when she switched off the computer. She had written four pages.

From then on she got up at six, before the heat set in, and wrote until ten. She soon discovered that writing was much harder than translating. When you translate, she explained later, someone else has already made the hard decisions: you only have to be faithful. When you write, on the other hand, nobody tells you what comes next. There were mornings when she wrote three pages and mornings when she spent four hours on a single sentence, moving a comma and putting it back where it had been.

She told no one. But Rosa Elena, who stayed the night with her on Tuesdays, caught her one morning writing in her pyjamas, with cold coffee beside her. She asked what she was doing. Ecaterina said she was writing a book. Rosa Elena thought for a moment and asked whether it was a real book, with covers, or just a computer one. Ecaterina replied that she didn’t know yet, that books become books little by little, just as people grow up.

Rosa Elena, for her part, announced that summer that she had already decided what she wanted to be when she grew up. She wanted to become a lorry driver, like Costel, and a translator, like Ecaterina. Both at once. When Mihai asked how she planned to do that, she explained very patiently that she would drive the lorry by day and translate books by night, in the cab, since that’s what the bed was for. Costel said it was the best career plan he had ever heard.

One Thursday, in the middle of the month, the power went off across the whole neighbourhood because of the heat. The club stayed on the balcony in the dark, with two candles Mrs Florica brought and the sound of air-conditioners switching off one after another. Ecaterina told them that on the night of 23 February 1981 they had sat just like this, in the bookshop, by candlelight, listening to the radio without knowing whether there would still be a democracy the next day. Costel said he spent many nights like that in the cab. Nobody switched on a phone until the power came back.

At the end of July an email arrived from Lola. She wrote that the café had turned into something else: since she had put the books from the funeral on the shelves, people no longer came just for coffee, but to read, to borrow books and to bring them back with notes inside. Without realising it, she had become a librarian. The neighbours already called the lamp at the back “Andrés’s lamp”. Ecaterina read the email aloud on the balcony, and nobody said anything for a while.

On 30 July, a day before the deadline, Marta sent the plaque text to the city council. They hadn’t changed a single comma: “Here stood the La Lámpara bookshop. Its bookseller, Andrés Gil, left the light on.” That night, the last Thursday in July, Ecaterina surprised everyone. As they were clearing away the glasses, she took some printed pages out of her bag, put on her glasses, although she no longer needed them, and said she wanted to read them something.

She read the first chapter. It was about a thirty-two-year-old woman arriving in Madrid on a rainy day, with a dictionary in her suitcase and the certainty that she would soon leave. It was about a bookshop with a green sign, a bookseller who offered her tea without asking her name, a city that had just woken up after forty years of silence. She read for twenty minutes. When she finished, it was night and the lights had come on in the balconies opposite.

Nobody clapped. Costel was crying, as always, but silently. Ana was the first to speak: she asked what the book was going to be called. Ecaterina folded the pages carefully, put them in her bag and said she wasn’t sure yet, but she had a working title: “The Lamp Left On”. Then she added, without looking at anyone, that perhaps, after all, at her age a person could still turn into something else. That all it took was for someone to leave a light on.

“dar por hecho” = to take for granted
“no me arrepiento” = I don’t regret it
“le vendría bien” = would do her good
“no se está quieta” = never keeps still

Write (at least 250 words) about how you have changed over the last five years, or how your town has changed. Use at least five different verbs of change.
I used “ponerse” for a momentary emotion.
I used “volverse” for a change of character.
I used “hacerse” for a deliberate change (a profession, a habit).
I used “convertirse en” or “llegar a ser” for an important transformation.
I used “quedarse” for the result of an event.
Five years ago I was very nervous at my first job interview; today I have become much more confident.
I became a vegetarian because of my sister and, little by little, cooking turned into my passion.
